pending_items.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming Israel govt
pending_items.content:
The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.

Delegations from Eisenkot's Yashar party and Netanyahu's Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.

"The latest round of coalition talks... has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail," the two parties said in a joint statement.

"A follow-up meeting will be held," they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details.

A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government, with the possibility of a 14‑day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.

His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra‑Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.

Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men, a mechanism already tried in Israel.

Such an arrangement could allow Netanyahu to keep his political protection against the corruption charges he faces, as well as continue to oppose the creation of an independent commission of inquiry into the security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.

But that prospect runs up against Eisenkot's refusal to serve in a cabinet led by Netanyahu, against whom he centred his campaign.

His ally Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister, also reiterated on Saturday his refusal to join a coalition with "Netanyahu or his bloc, under any circumstances".

On Saturday, Yashar presented the resumption of talks as "a genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government", saying that Eisenkot had asked his representatives to explore all options.

But Likud immediately laid down several conditions for its participation in a unity government, a formula backed by Netanyahu.

Among other things, it demands an end to "all personal attacks and incitement to hatred" targeting Netanyahu and his government.

It also called for bringing together "all the parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation‑state of the Jewish people", without the participation of Arab parties.

Netanyahu and his allies regularly target Arab parties, which secured a record 19 seats in the legislature and are opposed to Netanyahu remaining in power.

Likud is also demanding agreement on several major policy positions, notably rejecting the creation of a Palestinian state, maintaining Israeli control over territories in Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.

It is also pushing for a compromise on conscription of ultra‑Orthodox Jews, a particularly sensitive issue in Israel.

On Friday, Eisenkot warned that he would not allow the talks to drag on, saying he was ready to submit to parliament an "emergency national government".

Although he did not spell out how, his statements suggest a two‑stage plan: the swift formation of a minority government based on the core opposition parties, and then broadening it.

A minority Eisenkot government could receive support from the 19 Arab party lawmakers but Eisenkot's right-wing ally Avigdor Liberman rejects working with them and instead advocates an alliance with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Our correspondents are already on the next chapter. Read everything they file, from $2/week.

pending_items.title: Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
pending_items.content:
Israel will probably lose the genocide case brought by South Africa if the International Court of Justice (ICJ) applies the reasoning it used last week to find Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, an Israeli international law scholar has said.

“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.

“Before jumping to conspiracy theories about the court, Israel has mainly itself to blame,” he wrote in a series of posts in Hebrew on X. “Even if you disagree with the majority on every legal point, no reasonable country should come anywhere close to falling short of the standards it set. In many respects, Netanyahu’s government dug this hole itself.”

The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.

The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.

To prove the genocide, the ICJ first had to prove that genocidal acts were committed, then that there was a “specific intent” by the Myanmar state to destroy the group.

Genocidal intent is rarely ever stated explicitly, so courts usually rely on circumstantial evidence. And where there are various possible intentions, such as military objectives, the court then establishes whether genocide is the only reasonable explanation for the conduct.

Myanmar argued that its campaign against the Rohingya was a counter-insurgency operation and that other motives that could explain its conduct included a desire to drive the Rohingya out or to punish the civilian population.

But the court rejected all these explanations and said the “only reasonable inference” to be drawn from Myanmar’s conduct was genocide.

Lieblich argued that Israeli officials themselves have provided evidence of genocidal intent that is easier to prove than that in the Myanmar case.

'Given the statements by senior officials, the overall context and other aspects of the case, I think Israel would still most likely lose under the majority’s approach'

- Eliav Lieblich, Tel Aviv University

“The statements by senior Myanmar officials about the Rohingya that the court relied on seem mild compared with what has come out of the Netanyahu–Ben Gvir–Smotrich gang,” he said. “Add the rampage in the West Bank, and in my view Israel is in a very bad position.”

The nine judges in the majority found that the scale and pattern of the violence made an intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya the only reasonable inference.

The six dissenters accepted that Myanmar’s forces committed grave atrocities but took a narrower view of their proven scale and reach. They considered forced displacement a reasonable alternative explanation, which meant the test for proving genocidal intent was not met.

Lieblich said two parts of the majority’s interpretation of the Genocide Convention, taken together, “fundamentally undermine Israel’s position”.

The first concerns forced displacement. The court found that expelling people in harsh conditions and preventing them from returning home can cause the kind of serious mental harm covered by Article II(b) of the convention. The second concerns what it means to destroy a group.

In Lieblich’s reading, the required intent can include an aim to prevent the group from continuing to function as a group.

Lieblich said the implications for Gaza become clearer when Israel’s displacement of Palestinians and destruction of neighbourhoods are considered alongside conditions in the areas people fled to and statements by senior Israeli officials.

He referred to “a defining moment” when Avraham Zarbiv, a military reservist who operated a bulldozer in Gaza and publicly celebrated the demolitions, lit a torch at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony.

Lieblich said Israel could argue that Hamas’s military capabilities and the nature of the fighting in Gaza set the case apart from Myanmar’s campaign against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army.

Israel could also point to the scale of the 7 October attacks and argue that its actions were aimed at putting pressure on Hamas and destroying it.

“Given the statements by senior officials, the overall context and other aspects of the case, I think Israel would still most likely lose under the majority’s approach,” he said.

For Lieblich, the split between the judges reflected differences over how to assess the evidence, what constitutes genocide and how sharply the law should distinguish it from other grave crimes.

“Either way, anyone who, like Myanmar, has to defend themselves against accusations of genocide by arguing that their actions amounted to other serious crimes has already lost,” he wrote.

Lieblich said he was surprised to learn that Myanmar had set up a commission of inquiry that found serious crimes had been committed during the military operation. In his view, the inquiry did little to help Myanmar’s case because it did not adequately investigate the genocide allegation before the court.

“In Israel, even the opposition has yet to propose a commission of inquiry to examine these aspects,” he wrote.

The court held that Myanmar committed genocide against 815,000 Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, a region in western Myanmar along the border with Bangladesh. The figure amounts to roughly 58 percent of the 1.4 million Rohingya that Myanmar said lived in the country at the time.

The group targeted was large enough to constitute a “substantial part” of the Rohingya population under the Genocide Convention.

The court found three acts of genocide committed against men, women and children: the killing of 10,000 Rohingya, causing serious physical or psychological harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births.

The court confirmed what international law has previously held, that a state does not have to do everything it can to destroy the group, or to kill all its members, in order to be held responsible for genocide.

The ICJ also found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by individuals acting alongside its security forces, failed to punish genocide and other acts prohibited under the Genocide Convention, and failed to enact legislation giving effect to the treaty.

It also ruled that Myanmar breached one of the court’s four provisional measures, a 2020 order to preserve evidence, by building a government base on former Rohingya village sites and destroying the remains of at least five other villages.

pending_items.title: ‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
pending_items.content:
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).

“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.

“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”

The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.

It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.

Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.

Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.

In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.

Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.

Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.

Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.

A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.

By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.

The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.

Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.

The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.

The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.

Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.

A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.

According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.

Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.

Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.

Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.

In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.

July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.

By April 2024, Israel’s assault had destroyed all six of Gaza’s wastewater treatment plants. An estimated 40,000 cubic metres of raw sewage enter the Mediterranean daily, enough to fill 16 Olympic-size pools.

By April 2026, 19 percent of pumping stations and about 30 percent of the sewer network still functioned at least partly.

Gaza’s waste collection fleet fell from 261 vehicles to 48.

Both main landfills remained inaccessible. Of at least 56 temporary dumps, only 11 were accessible and operating.

These sites generally lack barriers to protect soil and groundwater. By April 2026, an estimated 1.45 million people lived in areas affected by rodents and other pests.

Before October 2023, Gaza’s farms supplied about 95 percent of the fresh vegetables people ate. By late 2025, more than 87 percent of cropland was damaged.

Oxfam says only 3 percent was accessible and undamaged.

By October 2024, the UN had reported that more than one million olive trees had been uprooted.

Oxfam identified more than 7,200 damaged greenhouses and documented the destruction of facilities that preserved and distributed Palestinian seeds.

Before the assault, Gaza’s fisheries produced about 4,660 tonnes of fish a year, with fish farms adding 750 tonnes.

In July 2026, an estimated 1.2 million people (59 percent) faced crisis levels of acute food shortages or worse, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, cited by the report.

The report also records the loss of roughly 95 percent of cattle and a collapse in fishing.

The average daily catch from October 2023 to April 2024 was 7.3 percent of its 2022 level. Oxfam warns that contaminants could enter crops and seafood as production resumes.

Gaza’s gross domestic product fell by 83 percent in 2024 to $362m, the report says.

Damage to farms, workshops and factories has stripped people of income and the means to resume work. Debris removal, repairs and farming could expose workers to asbestos, silica and other hazards for years.

Among the commerce and industry establishments assessed, 92 percent sustained damage, including 72 percent that were destroyed.

A joint World Bank, European Union and UN assessment, cited by Oxfam, put direct physical damage at $35.2bn and economic losses at $22.7bn by October 2025.

It estimated recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.4bn over a decade, including $26.3bn in the first 18 months.

Disease prevalence in Gaza recorded more than 1.9 million cases of acute respiratory infection and about 81,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in January and February 2026. More than 36,000 of the diarrhoea cases were among children aged below five years. Gaza recorded more than 496,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in 2025.

In 2024, vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 was detected in Gaza’s wastewater. A child was later diagnosed with paralytic polio, Gaza’s first reported case in 25 years. The report also cites the detection of multidrug-resistant pseudomonas in water at primary healthcare centres.
